# Persistent print issues: feasibility spike, second run

Date: 2026-10-08. Independent of the first report (`investigation-persistent-print-issues.md` in the main checkout); I read 60 lines of it before being asked to redo the work and did not use it.

This spike asked whether JusPrin can keep OrcaSlicer's current print problems visible outside the chat: highlight the affected object, anchor a bubble beside it, and send "Ask AI" or "Resolve with AI" to the existing chat. I built a working prototype and ran it through 39 lifecycle steps in the real application. **It works end to end, and it needs no change to any OrcaSlicer-owned file.**

This file and the folder `investigation-persistent-print-issues-run2/` are untracked on purpose. They live in the spike's worktree because this session may not write to the main checkout.

## Update, 2026-10-09: production candidate

Kenneth converted the spike into production work and made three decisions. This section is current; everything below it describes the first prototype and is kept for its findings. Where the two disagree, this section wins.

**Decisions taken**

- OrcaSlicer's own notices are hidden entirely while the JusPrin shell is installed.
- The compact status sits in the lower right corner of the Prepare canvas, where those notices were. Its list opens upward.
- The chat message quotes OrcaSlicer's text under the request sentence.

**Upstream footprint: 2 added lines, 0 changed, in 1 file.** In `NotificationManager::render_notifications`, after `sort_notifications()`:

```cpp
	if (wxGetApp().plater()->get_view3D_canvas3D()->legacy_overlays_hidden())
		return;
```

- It reuses the flag the shell already sets on the Prepare canvas at install and restores when the person switches back to the classic presentation, so there is no new member, setter or getter, and nothing new to save or restore. An earlier version of this work added a dedicated switch (6 lines in 2 files); Kenneth pointed out the existing flag covers it.
- It asks the Prepare canvas, not the canvas being drawn. The version that asked the drawn canvas (`canvas.legacy_overlays_hidden()`) was built and tested first: the Check print window is a second canvas whose own flag is never set, and it drew 7 notice windows there. Setting the flag on that canvas instead would also remove Check print's own stock controls. With the Prepare canvas as the question, Check print draws none.
- Skipping the draw does not disturb the notices' lifetimes: those advance in `update_notifications`, not in the draw.
- Rebase evidence: fork base `3ffb9585d2`, upstream `b3490a1cdc`, candidate commit object `6e97ea01e8` (on no branch). The conflict list is identical to the baseline's (3,890 both); `NotificationManager.cpp` has one conflict block before and after. In the merged result upstream's new `m_imgui_ready = true;` line runs first, then `sort_notifications()`, then the early return.
- The simulation is why the lines sit after `sort_notifications()` and not at the top of the function: at the top they collided with that new upstream line, and the wrong resolution would have skipped it.
- Upstream changes at the touched lines since the fork base and in two years: 1 and 1.
- What the fork owns: two lines that read an existing fork flag. No upstream line deleted or rewritten.

**What changed from the prototype**

- The reader now also covers OrcaSlicer's plate checks (TPU count, filament printability, PLA with PETG, nozzle and filament, filament mixture, prime tower outside the plate, a filament its nozzle cannot reach) and the post-slice checks (path outside the plate or above the print height, nozzle range and height errors, filament not printable on the plate). All through public OrcaSlicer functions or state.
- "Ask AI may only read" is now enforced by the chat host itself, not only by the model provider adapter.
- Typed messages and button messages share one path in the chat host.
- The two bubble widths are tokens with guards. All strings go through translation.
- Bubble and status placement is a separate unit with its own tests.
- The long list scrolls instead of leaving the canvas.
- With no assistant set up, a press of either button sends nothing to the chat. A dialog says "The AI assistant isn't set up yet. Set it up in the chat panel, and it can explain this issue and help you fix it." with **Set up now** (opens the chat panel's setup) and **Not now**.

## The answer

**Can we keep current print issues visible and actionable outside chat without taking ownership of Orca's warning logic?** Yes. Demonstrated at runtime, not only argued from code.

**What native access is missing?** Nothing that needs an upstream edit. One native fact, the reason a slice failed, exists only inside an event that OrcaSlicer defines in `Plater.cpp` and declares in no header. A declaration placed in a fork-owned header that `Plater.cpp` already includes makes that event observable. Upstream line count: 0.

**What would the fork permanently own?**

- A *reader* that asks OrcaSlicer's own checks what is wrong, and decides when to ask again. It owns no rule about what counts as a problem.
- The list of native sources it reads (six today, see the table). A new kind of native warning is invisible until someone adds a reader for it. This is the real permanent cost.
- The pill, list and bubble on the canvas, and their layout rules.
- One chat entry point for a message sent by a button outside the page, plus the "explain only" tool limit.
- The tests that pin all of the above to OrcaSlicer's behaviour.

Uncommitted, in worktree `.claude/worktrees/wonderful-roentgen-83d009` (branch `claude/persistent-print-issues-spike-9238a1`, at `jusprin-newui` commit `198c64606f`). 17 files, none of which exists in upstream. About 1,050 lines of product code and 1,050 lines of test code.

|---|---|---|
| Issue reader | `src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/PrintIssues/PrintIssueMonitor.{hpp,cpp}` | Builds the current issue list for the active plate from native state. Recomputes on five existing signals. |
| Canvas overlay | `src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/PrintIssues/IssueOverlay.{hpp,cpp}` | Status pill, issue list, and the anchored bubble with both buttons. Drawn with ImGui through the overlay hook the tool strip already uses. |

## Verdicts

### Anchored, clickable overlay: verified working

- **Rendering owner.** ImGui inside the Prepare canvas's own frame, through `GLCanvas3D::set_overlay_renderer`. That hook is an existing fork seam. No web content over the GL canvas, no extra window.
- **Position.** The anchor is the top centre of the target copy's bounding box, projected with the camera every frame. Nothing about position is stored. The test computes the projection separately and compares: equal to within 1.5 px after orbit, zoom, window resize and object move.
- **Clicks.** Real pointer events through the canvas's mouse handler and ImGui's hit test press both buttons, the pager and a list row. ImGui takes the pointer first, so a click on the bubble never reaches selection or the camera.
- **Beside, never on top.** The bubble goes above the object when there is room. Otherwise it takes the object's right, left or underside, whichever fits inside the canvas without covering the object, the pill, the open list or the tool strip. The first version only slid the bubble down to fit and covered the object when it was near the top of the view; Kenneth caught that by hand on 2026-10-09. A test now reproduces it (it failed before the fix) and passes (`issues-05c-object-near-top.png`).
- **Edges.** When the object is off screen or behind the camera, or fills the view so no side is free, the bubble docks under the pill rather than disappearing.
- **Highlight.** Selecting an issue selects its copy through the existing `select_copy` command, by OrcaSlicer's instance ID. With two objects of the same name, the right one is selected.

Not verified: display scaling other than this Mac's 2x, Windows and Linux, dark mode, gizmo dragging while a bubble is open.

### Existing chat submission: verified working, with fork-owned additions

Path traced and exercised: button click → `ShellController::submit_issue` → `AgentHost::submit_issue_message` → message appended to the project document → `message_added` to the page → `begin_reply` → `AgentRequest`.

- The message is an ordinary user message. The real chat page drew it with no page change (`08-asked-chat.png`).
- The structured context travels beside the text and reaches the model as labelled source data. Fields sent: issue id, source, severity, native code, setting key, Orca's message; target scope, object ID, copy ID, object name, plate ID; whether Orca has validated, the evidence generation, sliced and slicing flags; workspace session ID and revision. The whole workspace snapshot already goes with every request.
- The composer draft is left alone. The closed chat pane is opened.
- **Missing before this prototype:** any way for native UI to send a user message, and any place on a message to carry context. Both are fork-owned additions (about 70 lines).

### End to end: verified

Warning appears → object highlights → bubble tracks the object and view → each button submits the right visible message and context → native revalidation updates or removes the bubble. Also verified with object deletion and with several issues at once. 334 checks, 0 failures.

## Source and coverage table

"Re-asked" means the reader calls the same public native function OrcaSlicer calls. "Read" means it reads state OrcaSlicer already stores.

| Native source | Example reproduced | Blocks printing natively? | Where the truth lives | Target identity | Goes stale / clears | Prototype |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `Print::validate` error | Two cubes 2 mm apart with "By object" sequence; vase mode with two objects | Yes. Plate marked invalid, Slice disabled | Not stored. Re-asked on the plate's `Print` | Copy ID, object ID, or none plus a setting key | Stale for up to 500 ms after an edit; cleared by Orca's next validation | Verified |
| `Print::validate` warning | The handoff's "is too close to others" (by-layer mode) | No | Not stored. Re-asked | Copy ID of the first offender only | Same | Verified |
| Copy over the plate edge | Cube straddling the edge | Yes | `ModelInstance::print_volume_state`, read | Copy ID | Same | Verified |
| Slicing step warnings | "has floating cantilever" on an overhang | No | `Print` and `PrintObject` step state, with Orca's own `current` flag, read | Object ID | Orca marks it not current when its step is invalidated; removed by the next slice | Verified |
| Slice result | "Found gcode path conflicts between…" | No | `Print::get_conflict_result`, slice result warnings, read | Copy ID or none | Gone when the slice is invalidated | Verified (conflict). G-code processor warnings are read but none was reproduced |
| Slicing failure | "No layers were detected" on a 0.02 mm slab | Yes | **Only in the completion event** | Object ID when the error carries one; this one does not | Stale when the project changes; dropped when a slice starts | Verified |
| Plate checks the canvas runs | Filament, TPU, nozzle and mixture compatibility | Some | Public `PartPlate::check_*` functions, re-askable | Plate-wide | Same as validation | **Not prototyped.** Building block confirmed in code only |
| Post-slice bounds | Toolpath beyond plate or height | Yes | Slice result; the fork's `slice_report` already recomputes one | Plate-wide | With the slice | **Not prototyped** |
| Operation errors | Network and download errors pushed as notifications | n/a | Notification only | n/a | n/a | Verified absent from the list |

The "unfamiliar warning" case needs no special handling: the reader has no explanation for any warning. Every entry is Orca's own text plus identifiers, so an unknown one is carried the same way as a known one.

## Native behaviour that shapes the design

Each of these was observed at runtime or read in code, and each changes what the product can promise.

1. **OrcaSlicer's validation holds one error and one warning at most.** A later check overwrites an earlier warning (`Print.cpp:1261` has a FIXME saying so). Several offending objects become one message with several lines and one target. "Several validation findings on one object" cannot happen natively.
2. **A copy over the plate edge is dropped from validation.** With both overlapping cubes over the edge, Orca reported two placement blockers and no clearance warning.
3. **A slice warning survives a plain move.** Moving the object invalidates the slice result but not the step that produced the warning, so Orca still vouches for it. Changing the setting the step depends on (`enable_support`) makes it not current. Only the next slice removes it.
4. **A move made during a slice does not cancel it.** Orca's log shows `apply result=1` (changed, not invalidated) and the slice finished valid. The reader reports Orca's verdict; it does not second-guess it.
5. **Popups are not a list of issues.** Closing a popup removes it while the issue stays true (`issues-07-popup-dismissed.png`). Orca merges slicing warnings that share a message ID into one popup across objects. Targets are captured inside callbacks and cannot be read. Popups are not retired at all while the window is inactive (the count grew from 3 to 10 in one run).
6. **Orca applies an edit to the print on a 500 ms timer.** Until then the print describes the old project. `Plater::is_background_process_update_scheduled()` is public and tells the reader exactly this. It is what makes "checking" distinguishable from "no issues".
7. **Validation exists only for the active plate.** Other plates are unknown until visited.
8. **The warning's `type` field is uninitialised in some producers** (`StringObjectException warningtemp;` in `Print.cpp`). The reader reports a type only when it is one Orca defines, and never uses it for identity.
9. **Validation costs 0.2 to 0.9 ms** on these fixtures, so asking a second time is cheap here. Not measured on a large plate.

## Lifecycle results

All from `investigation-persistent-print-issues-run2/harness-run.log`.

| Case | Result |
|---|---|
| Creation | Issue appears after Orca's own validation, with copy ID |
| Repeated updates | Same issue ID after each revalidation; no duplicates |
| Popup dismissed | Issue stays |
| Edit, before Orca revalidates | List marked stale, pill says "Checking…", buttons off, a forced submit returns `unchecked` |
| Fix, then revalidation | Issue and bubble removed. No "No print issues" shown before the check |
| Undo / redo | Undo brings back the same issue ID on the same copy; redo clears it |
| Object deleted with its bubble open | Its issues go at once, before revalidation; bubble closes; submit returns `expired` |
| Plate switch | List follows the active plate and returns on switching back |
| Project replaced | New session, empty list; an old issue ID cannot be submitted |
| Slice warning, remedy applied, not yet resliced | Shown stale; cannot be submitted; removed only by the new slice |
| Slice fails | Reason listed as a blocker; stale after an edit |
| Edit during a slice | Reader matches Orca's final verdict; no false failure |
| Duplicate object names | Correct copy selected by ID |
| Several issues | Three issues on two objects; one bubble pages through both findings on one object; the list shows all |
| Plate-wide issue | Docked bubble labelled "Whole plate"; no object invented |
| Object near the top edge, no room above | Bubble placed below the object; does not cover it or the tool strip |
| Chat pane closed | Opened on submit |
| Reply running | Buttons off; a forced press sends nothing; the host itself queues a message that arrives mid-reply |
| Agent unavailable | Status keeps working; the question is kept and the reply fails visibly with `agent_unavailable` |
| Same button pressed twice, nothing changed | One message |

Regression: the existing shell scenario passes with the prototype (526 checks), and `agent_bridge_tests` passes (4,691 assertions).

## Intent and permissions

- **Ask AI** sends "Explain this issue and my options." with `intent: explain`. For that turn the request names only the tools whose registry class is read-only (13 today). `OpenAIResponsesAgent` uses that list both to advertise tools and to refuse a call to any other (`OpenAIResponsesAgent.cpp:298`). So the limit is enforced by the app, not by wording.
- **Resolve with AI** sends "Help fix this issue." with `intent: resolve` and the ordinary tool set. It adds no tool and removes no check.
- A follow-up typed by the person is a normal turn with normal tools.

Gaps: the limit is applied by the provider adapter, not by `AgentHost` itself, so another adapter would have to honour it too. A host-level refusal is a small hardening step. I did not run a live model, so how well the model uses the context, and whether its words stay within "explain", is unverified. That needs an API key and sends project data to the provider, which I did not do without being asked.

## Options compared

Fork base `3ffb9585d2`, upstream `b3490a1cdc` (local `upstream/main`, not re-fetched).

| Option | Upstream lines | Upstream sites | Upstream changes at those sites since the fork base / in 2 years | Meets the requirements? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **1. Read native state and re-ask native checks (prototype)** | 0 | 0 | n/a | Yes, as tested |
| 1b. Same, declaring the event in `Plater.hpp` | 2 | 2 | 0 / 0 on those lines | Yes. Measured: adds one conflict block against current upstream, resolved by keeping both |
| 2. Read the notification manager | about 15 | 1 new accessor | `push_notification_data`: 2 / 3 | No. Loses targets, loses dismissed issues, merges objects |
| 3. Record results at the producers | 22 added, 3 removed in the first run's prototype, 9 hunks in `Plater.cpp` | `update_background_process`, `validate_current_plate`, `on_process_completed` | 2 / 10, 3 / 13, 6 / 7 | Likely yes, at a recurring rebase cost in the busiest file the fork touches |

Option 3's numbers are a measurement of the first run's uncommitted diff, not a review of it.

What option 1 depends on, and how it fails if upstream changes it:

- `Print::validate`'s signature and `PartPlate::fff_print()`. Compile error.
- `EVT_PROCESS_COMPLETED` staying a non-static definition in `Plater.cpp`. Compile or link error.
- `Plater::is_background_process_update_scheduled()`. Compile error. Unchanged upstream for at least two years.
- `get_object_clashed_text()`, declared in no header. Link error.
- The meaning of the 500 ms timer. **Silent** if upstream replaces the timer with something else: the reader would call unchecked state checked. The lifecycle test "no all-clear before revalidation" is the guard.
- Any step upstream adds before or after its own validation call. **Silent**, text-only drift between the popup and the bubble.

Merge simulation, `git merge-tree --write-tree --merge-base=3ffb9585d2 upstream/main <commit>`: the baseline (`198c64606f`) has 3,890 conflicts, almost all inherited release-branch history. With the final prototype (commit object `61c2352356`, on no branch) the conflict list is identical. None of the 17 changed files exists in upstream.

## Proposed behaviour

Required:

- One compact status that says one of three things: checking, no issues, or N issues with the number that block. Never "no issues" while Orca has not validated.
- A list of every issue, opened from the status.
- One bubble at a time, for the selected issue, beside its object and never covering it. All findings on that object share the bubble through a pager.
- A docked bubble for plate-wide issues and for objects out of view.
- Both buttons off while Orca has not validated the latest edit and while a reply is running.
- Context resolved at the click. Expired and unchecked issues are not sent.
- Orca's words shown unchanged.

Optional polish: an edge arrow toward an off-screen object, plain-language rewrites of Orca's text, a context chip on the chat message instead of the quoted text.

The prototype's pill sits on the canvas. The product home for the compact status is the header's status row, which already has the button and menu pieces. That is ordinary UI work, not a feasibility question, and I did not build it.

## Smallest implementation scope

1. Promote the reader, with the two unprototyped sources added.
2. Header status control in place of the canvas pill.
3. The bubble, to the design system. It uses theme colours and button recipes now, but two widths are literals that need tokens, and the text is ImGui's default font.
4. `submit_issue_message` plus a host-level check of the explain-only limit.
5. Turn the 39-step scenario into a kept harness mode.

Acceptance tests: the lifecycle table above, each row as a harness check, plus the two silent-drift guards named under option 1.

## Decisions for Kenneth

1. **Where the compact status lives.** Header (recommended) or canvas.
2. **What the visible chat message contains.** The prototype quotes Orca's message under the fixed sentence so the chat reads sensibly later. The alternative is the fixed sentence plus a chip, which needs page work.
3. **Agent unavailable.** The prototype follows existing chat behaviour: the question is kept and the reply fails with a retry. The alternative is disabled buttons with a route to agent setup.
4. **Pressing the same button again with nothing changed.** The prototype treats it as the same question and sends nothing.
5. **Other plates.** Show only the active plate (prototype), or mark the others "not checked".
6. **Whether to run a live-model check.** It needs your API key and sends the test project to the provider.

## Not verified

- Live model behaviour for either button.
- Windows, Linux, dark mode, other display scales.
- The two unprototyped sources in the table.
- Large plates (validation cost, bubble overlap with many objects).
- A slicing failure that names its object. The one reproduced carries no object ID natively.
- A click landing in the same event-loop turn as a committed move. In that turn neither native flag is set yet. Real input cannot reach it, because the click handler is queued behind the move's own event; this is reasoning, not a test.

## Reproduce

Build `shell_integration_harness` in the worktree, then run with a scratch `HOME`:

```bash
build/arm64/tests/shell/RelWithDebInfo/JusPrinShellHarness.app/Contents/MacOS/JusPrinShellHarness --print-issues-capture <output-dir>
```

`--manual-print-issues` leaves two overlapping cubes open for hands-on use.

109:### Print issues
110-
111-What is wrong with the active plate stays on the Prepare canvas whether or not the chat is open: a status pill in the canvas's lower right corner, the list it opens, and a bubble beside the object the selected issue is about, with **Ask AI** and **Resolve with AI**. OrcaSlicer's own notices are not drawn while the shell is installed.
112-
113-| Piece | Owns |
114-|---|---|
115-| `PrintIssues/PrintIssueMonitor` | The list. It asks OrcaSlicer's own checks again and reads the state OrcaSlicer already stores; it holds no rule about what a problem is. An entry exists while its native source reports it, and is marked stale while OrcaSlicer has an edit it has not yet applied to the print. |
116-| `PrintIssues/PrintIssue.hpp` | The entry: OrcaSlicer's words unchanged, a severity taken from whether OrcaSlicer itself refuses to slice or print, and the object and copy ids OrcaSlicer named. Ids come from the native source's identifiers, never from the message text. |
117-| `PrintIssues/IssueOverlayLayout` | Where the pieces go, as plain geometry with its own tests. The bubble goes above its object, else right, left, or below; it never covers the object, the pill, the open list, or the tool strip, and docks beside the pill when no side is free or the issue has no object. |
118-| `PrintIssues/IssueOverlay` | Drawing and input, with ImGui inside the canvas's frame through the same overlay hook as the tool strip. Position is recomputed from the camera every frame. |
119-| `PrintIssues/IssueContext` | The chat message a button sends: the request sentence, OrcaSlicer's words quoted beneath it, and the issue, its target and the freshness of the evidence as data for the model. |
120-| `AgentHost::submit_issue_message` | The one way a message enters the chat from outside the page. It shares the page's path, obeys the same refusals, and leaves the composer's draft alone. |
121-
122-Rules that follow from the above:
123-
124-- **Never "no issues" before a check.** While OrcaSlicer holds an unapplied edit the status says it is checking and both buttons are off.
125-- **Nothing is resolved by the fork.** An issue goes when OrcaSlicer stops reporting it. Closing a notice, pressing a button, or an agent saying it fixed something changes nothing.
126-- **A press acts on what is true at the press.** The issue is looked up again; one that has cleared or gone stale is not sent.
127-- **With no assistant set up, a press sends nothing.** It says so and offers to open the chat panel's setup; a question in the chat would only fail there.
128-- **Ask AI may only read.** The turn is offered the read-only tools and `AgentHost` refuses a call to any other, whatever the service asks for. Resolve with AI is an ordinary turn with no extra authority.
129-- **A new kind of native warning needs a reader.** With OrcaSlicer's notices hidden, a warning the monitor does not read is not shown anywhere. After an upstream update, check `GLCanvas3D::EWarning`, `NotificationType`, and the callers of the notification manager's `push_*` functions for sources the monitor lacks. Known gap: the "flushing volume set to 0" warning, whose check is private to `GLCanvas3D`.
130-- **Operation notices are not print issues.** Export finished, upload and download progress, update and network notices have no JusPrin surface yet; hiding OrcaSlicer's notices hides them too.
131-
132-### Agent WebView
133-
134-The production Agent interface is a standalone local React/TypeScript package embedded in `wxWebView`. It requires:
135-
136-- a versioned command/event schema;
137-- deterministic mock conversations for UI tests;
138-- incremental message rendering and stable scroll anchoring;
139-- explicit keyboard, focus, shortcut, clipboard, selection, and IME rules;
140-- reload, startup, bridge-error, and unavailable-agent states;
141-- no direct ownership of Orca project state.
142-
143-#### Where logic goes: the page first
144-
145-When the same logic could live either in C++ or in a React page, put it in the page unless there is a strong reason for C++. The page is quicker to change (Vite hot reload instead of relinking a multi-gigabyte GUI library), its tests run in milliseconds under Vitest, and it is already where the words people read are written. The words the model reads belong there too.
146-
147-Strong reasons for C++:
148-
149-- **It reads or changes OrcaSlicer state:** presets, the model, plates, slicing, the device list. The page never owns project state (see the constraints below).

235:### Print problems are read back from OrcaSlicer, not recorded as they pass
236-
237-OrcaSlicer reports print problems through three unrelated producers (print
238-validation in `Plater`, slicing steps on the background thread, plate checks in
239-`GLCanvas3D`), and all three end in `NotificationManager`. The notices are a
240-presentation, not a record: a closed notice is gone while its problem remains,
241-several objects' warnings are merged into one notice, and the object a notice
242-is about is captured inside a callback nobody else can read.
243-`PrintIssues/PrintIssueMonitor` therefore reads the facts where OrcaSlicer
244-keeps them, and changes no OrcaSlicer function to do it.
245-
246-- **Validation is asked again.** `Print::validate` is public and `const`, and
247-  `PartPlate::fff_print()` hands out the plate's print. It costs under a
248-  millisecond on small plates. It returns one error and one warning at most:
249-  a later check overwrites an earlier warning, and several offending objects
250-  become one message with one target. The warning's `type` is left
251-  uninitialised by some producers, so never use it for identity.
252-- **The print lags the project by up to 500 ms.** An edit schedules
253-  OrcaSlicer's update of the print on a timer.
254-  `Plater::is_background_process_update_scheduled()` is true until it runs;
255-  until then nothing read from the print describes the project as it is. This
256-  is what separates "checking" from "no issues".
257-- **A copy over the plate's edge is dropped from validation.** It gets a
258-  placement error instead and no clearance warning.
259-- **Step warnings carry their own freshness.** `step_state_with_warnings`
260-  keeps a warning whose step was invalidated, with `current == false`, until
261-  the step runs again. A plain move invalidates the slice result but not the
262-  object's steps, so the warning stays current; changing a setting the step
263-  depends on does not.
264-- **A move during a slice does not cancel it.** `Print::apply` reports
265-  "changed", not "invalidated", and the slice finishes valid.
266-- **Why a slice failed exists only in `EVT_PROCESS_COMPLETED`**, which
267-  `Plater.cpp` defines and no header declares. `Workspace/PlaterProjectState.hpp`
268-  declares it; `Plater.cpp` includes that header ahead of the definition, so
269-  the event gets external linkage with no OrcaSlicer line changed. The
270-  completion handler bound later runs first and must `Skip()`.
271-- **OrcaSlicer validates only the active plate.**
272-- **The notification manager stops retiring notices while its window is
273-  inactive**, so a count of notices only grows there.
274-
275-OrcaSlicer's notices are not drawn while the shell is installed.
276-`NotificationManager::render_notifications` returns early when the Prepare
277-canvas has its legacy overlays hidden, the flag the shell already sets on
278-install and restores on detach, so nothing new has to be saved or put back.
279-It asks the Prepare canvas rather than the canvas being drawn on purpose: the
280-Check print window is a second canvas whose own flag is never set, and asking
281-it would bring the notices back there. Only the drawing stops. Notices are
282-still pushed, timed out and closed, because that lifecycle runs in
283-`update_notifications`.
284-
285-### Application teardown can re-enter destroyed owners
286-
287-Quitting while model volumes are loaded can crash:
288-`~GLCanvas3D → reset_volumes → Selection::clear → Plater::canvas3D()` runs
289-after `Plater::priv` is destroyed and dereferences null. This is inherited
290-upstream behavior — crash reports with the identical signature predate the
291-JusPrin shell (2026-08-28) and the stock-mode harness reproduces it with all
292-fork runtime code inert. Until it is fixed in upstream teardown ordering,
293-automated GUI scenarios should end on an empty project (`new_project`) before
294-exiting; both harnesses do.
295-

55:## 1.1 The agent cannot observe physical reality reliably

content.content:
# 2. The surfaces that must remain

## 2.0 Project-window hierarchy

The Project window should not treat Prepare, Preview, and Info as three equal destinations.

- **Prepare is the dominant, persistent workspace.** It is where users inspect the model, communicate intent, manipulate geometry, resolve uncertainty, and review the agent's plan.
- **Check print opens Orca Preview in a modal window.** Prepare remains underneath; closing Check returns focus to Prepare. It is a secondary action when the active plate has a valid slice.
- **Info becomes Project details.** It is a drawer opened from the project name or menu. The agent reads its contents continuously even when the drawer is closed.
- **Print opens Send preflight.** It never sends directly. Explicit Send remains the consequential commitment.

The normal flow is:

`Prepare -> Check print -> return to Prepare if correction is needed -> Print -> Send preflight -> explicit Send`

### Default Project-window composition

The default window should contain:

- Project name and saved/unsaved state
- Compact printer pointer: target printer, nozzle, build plate, and material
- Compact, editable intent summary
- Compact active plate/object summary
- 3D Prepare canvas
- Essential direct-manipulation tools
- Compact pinned agent plan
- Highest unresolved assumption, compromise, or risk
- Check print
- Print
- Consequential warnings when applicable

The canvas is the primary human-agent collaboration surface. It must make the build plate and model visible, support camera rotation, pan, zoom, selection, and direct spatial manipulation, and show the changes the agent makes.

The compact summaries should keep the governing assumptions visible without expanding full editors. Examples:

> Decorative · appearance first · protect front surface · under 5 hours

> Plate 1 · Fuzzy Heart · 1 copy · PLA Matte

A one-object project should not permanently display a large object tree. A complete intent questionnaire should not remain expanded after it has been answered.

### Direct resolution of uncertainty
......
## 2.9 Print preflight

This surface answers: **Is the correct job about to be sent to the correct physical machine?**

Prepare should contain a visible Print entry point. Print opens this preflight; it does not bypass it:

`Print -> Send preflight -> explicit Send`

The current Print action opens Orca's existing Select Machine or printer-host send dialog, which requires a separate send/upload choice. The complete JusPrin preflight checklist below remains future product work.

### What should remain

- Job name and thumbnail
- Destination printer
- Selected plate
- Time and material estimate
- Filament and AMS mapping
- Plate-type confirmation
- Bed-leveling choice
- Flow-calibration choice
- Timelapse choice
- First-layer inspection
- Build-plate detection
- Tangle and clumping detection
- AI-monitoring behavior and sensitivity
- Recovery options
- Warnings about disabled checks
- Explicit Send control
......
## 2.12 Privacy, updates, portability, and expert administration

These functions are used less frequently, but they are important for particular users and organizations.

### User-owned decisions

- Cloud login region
- Stealth or offline mode
- Network-plugin use
- Preset synchronization
- Multi-device management
- Firmware and application update timing
- Camera and monitoring privacy
- Backup and recovery policy
- Importing and replacing configurations
- Ownership and export of project data

### Capabilities that should remain available

- Import 3MF, STL, STEP, SVG, OBJ, AMF, ZIP archives, and configurations
- Export models, projects, sliced plates, G-code, and preset bundles
- Export printer, filament, and process profiles
- Manage downloaded and stored printer files
- Access timelapses
- Run network diagnostics
- Open configuration data
- Enable developer tools

### Why the agent cannot decide these alone

These choices affect privacy, compatibility, organizational policy, intellectual property, and the user’s ability to leave the product.

The agent can simplify the workflows, but it should not silently enable cloud communication, install firmware, replace profiles, or trap projects in a proprietary format.

---

# 3. Recommended final product structure
......
## 3.5 Overlays and application-level layers

- **Send preflight:** final job, destination, material mapping, safety, and monitoring confirmation followed by explicit Send
- **Expert layer:** raw process settings, numeric per-object and per-region overrides, manual calibration ranges, toolpath diagnostics, and G-code
- **Preferences:** cloud region, stealth/offline behavior, network plugins, sync, updates, privacy, backup and recovery, import/export administration, and developer tools

This structure preserves the lifecycle of a print without turning Setup, Intent, Plan, Verify, Print, Monitor, and Diagnose into nine equal screens.

---

# 4. Visibility hierarchy

## 4.1 Default

Continuously visible in the ordinary Project window:

- Project name and saved/unsaved state
- Current printer, nozzle, plate, and material summary
- Compact intent summary
- Compact active plate and object summary
- 3D Prepare canvas
- Add, remove, select, move, rotate, scale, place on face, arrange, duplicate, Undo, and Redo
- Compact agent plan
- Highest unresolved assumption or risk
- Check print and Print

Inside Check, the default changes to sliced appearance, time, material, cost, the highest-priority warning, and comparison with intent. When supports exist, support placement and removal risk become the default Check emphasis.

## 4.2 Contextual

Shown when the project or current task makes it relevant:

- Full object, part, and plate tree
- Per-object material or extruder
- Modifiers, support enforcers, blockers, print order, and search
- Local surface annotations and object-specific requirements
- Mirror, cut, split, merge, assemble, text, measure, repair, positive/negative parts, and multi-plate distribution
- Seam, bridge, overhang, thin-feature, first-layer, island, and collision inspection
- Material changes, purge waste, prime tower, and extruder assignments
- Time and material estimate in Prepare after a valid background slice exists
- Assembly instructions, accessories, and reference pictures
- Calibration and maintenance recommendations
- Firmware updates, storage, timelapses, and multi-device management

## 4.3 On demand

Available through Project details, More, or the expert layer:

- Full intent questionnaire after it has been completed
- Project description, author, license, pictures, BOM, assembly guide, and profile notes
- Version, backup, ownership, and export administration
- Detailed agent rationale, alternatives, confidence, profile deviations, and change history
- Individual speeds and accelerations
- Exact line widths
- Infill and support implementation parameters
- Retraction, wiping, cooling, and purge details
- Complete toolpath legend and playback
- Raw G-code
- Manual calibration ranges
- Network tests, configuration folders, developer mode, and visualization preferences

## 4.4 Interruptive

Normally hidden, but presented prominently at the point where the user can resolve it:

- Wrong printer, nozzle, plate, or filament
- Safety or usage instruction relevant to the current plan
- Unsupported, missing, or defective geometry
- Support entering a protected region
- Violated dimensional requirement
- Material incompatible with the stated use
- Agent uncertainty about a meaning-changing geometry operation
- License conflict during sharing, publishing, commercial use, or export
- Unsaved work, recovery issue, or version conflict
- Printer-health or safety alert

---

# CLAUDE.md - Testing Guide for OrcaSlicer

This guide provides comprehensive instructions for Claude Code when writing, maintaining, and understanding tests in the OrcaSlicer codebase.

## ⚠️ CRITICAL RULES - MUST FOLLOW

### 1. **SECTIONS IN LOOPS - NEVER REUSE NAMES**
❌ **WRONG**: Will cause unpredictable behavior
```cpp
TEST_CASE("Bad loop sections") {
    for (int i = 0; i < 3; ++i) {
        SECTION("Same name") {  // WRONG! Same name used multiple times
            REQUIRE(i >= 0);
        }
    }
}
```

✅ **CORRECT**: Use DYNAMIC_SECTION or incorporate counter
```cpp
TEST_CASE("Good loop sections") {
    for (int i = 0; i < 3; ++i) {
        DYNAMIC_SECTION("Section " << i) {  // Unique name per iteration
            REQUIRE(i >= 0);
        }
    }
}
```

### 2. **THREAD SAFETY - ASSERTIONS ARE NOT THREAD-SAFE**
❌ **WRONG**: Will cause undefined behavior or crashes
```cpp
TEST_CASE("Multi-threaded test") {
    std::vector<std::thread> threads;
    for (int i = 0; i < 4; ++i) {
        threads.emplace_back([]() {
            REQUIRE(some_calculation() == expected);  // NOT THREAD-SAFE!
        });
    }
}
```

✅ **CORRECT**: Synchronize results, test on main thread
```cpp
TEST_CASE("Multi-threaded test") {
    std::vector<std::thread> threads;
    std::atomic<int> passed{0};
    
    for (int i = 0; i < 4; ++i) {
        threads.emplace_back([&passed]() {
            if (some_calculation() == expected) {
                passed++;
            }
        });
    }
    
    for (auto& t : threads) t.join();
    REQUIRE(passed == 4);  // Test results on main thread
}
```

### 3. **EXPRESSION DECOMPOSITION - AVOID BINARY OPERATORS**
❌ **WRONG**: Cannot decompose properly
```cpp
REQUIRE(a > 0 && b < 10);  // Shows "false" on failure, not individual values
```

✅ **CORRECT**: Split into separate assertions
```cpp
REQUIRE(a > 0);
REQUIRE(b < 10);  // Each shows individual values on failure
```

### 4. **FLOATING POINT - NEVER USE APPROX**
❌ **WRONG**: Approx is deprecated and asymmetric
```cpp
REQUIRE(calculated_value == Catch::Approx(expected));  // Deprecated!
```

✅ **CORRECT**: Use floating point matchers
```cpp
REQUIRE_THAT(calculated_value, WithinAbs(expected, 0.001));
REQUIRE_THAT(calculated_value, WithinRel(expected, 0.01));  // 1% tolerance
REQUIRE_THAT(calculated_value, WithinULP(expected, 4));     // 4 ULPs apart
```

### 5. **TEST ORDERING - ALWAYS USE RANDOM ORDER**
✅ **REQUIRED**: For CI/CD and development
```bash
# Essential flags for running tests
./tests --order rand --warn NoAssertions

# For test sharding (parallel execution), share random seed
./tests --order rand --shard-index 0 --shard-count 3 --rng-seed 0xBEEF
./tests --order rand --shard-index 1 --shard-count 3 --rng-seed 0xBEEF
./tests --order rand --shard-index 2 --shard-count 3 --rng-seed 0xBEEF
```

## Overview of OrcaSlicer's Testing Framework

OrcaSlicer uses **Catch2 v3** (currently v3.11.0, vendored in `tests/catch2/`) as its primary testing framework. The test suite is organized into several modules that mirror the project's architectural components:

> **Note**: Test files include the framework via `#include <catch2/catch_all.hpp>` (the v3 single-header convenience include). All v3 features described in this guide are available.

```
tests/
```

## Catch2 Features Guide

### Basic Assertions
```cpp

REQUIRE_FALSE(expression);

// Continuing assertions - continue test after failure  
CHECK(expression);
CHECK_FALSE(expression);

// Non-failing checks - record result but don't fail test

```

### Exception Testing
```cpp

REQUIRE_NOTHROW(function_call());

// Verify any exception is thrown

// Verify specific exception type
REQUIRE_THROWS_AS(function_call(), SpecificException);

// Verify exception message
REQUIRE_THROWS_WITH(function_call(), "Expected error message");

// Verify exception with matchers (for partial matching)
```

### Complex Assertions with Matchers
```cpp

// String matchers

using Catch::Matchers::EndsWith;

using Catch::Matchers::Equals;

REQUIRE_THAT(float_value, WithinULP(expected, 4));         // ULP difference (requires IEEE-754)
```

## Common Pitfalls and Solutions

### Floating-Point Comparisons

> **CRITICAL**: Never use Approx - it's deprecated due to asymmetry and other issues

❌ **Incorrect**:
```cpp
REQUIRE(calculated_volume == expected_volume);           // Exact equality
REQUIRE(calculated_volume == Catch::Approx(expected));   // Deprecated! Asymmetric!
```

✅ **Correct**: Always use floating point matchers
```cpp
// Absolute tolerance - good when values are near zero
REQUIRE_THAT(calculated_volume, WithinAbs(expected_volume, 0.001));

// Relative tolerance - good for values with different magnitudes
REQUIRE_THAT(calculated_volume, WithinRel(expected_volume, 0.01));  // 1% tolerance

// ULP (Units in Last Place) - most precise, requires IEEE-754
REQUIRE_THAT(calculated_volume, WithinULP(expected_volume, 4));

// Combined approach - relative OR absolute
REQUIRE_THAT(calculated_volume, 
    WithinRel(expected_volume, 0.001) || WithinAbs(0.0, 0.000001));

// Precision control for output
Catch::StringMaker<double>::precision = 15;  // Show more decimal places
```

### Why Approx is Problematic:
- **Asymmetric**: `Approx(10).epsilon(0.1) != 11.1` but `Approx(11.1).epsilon(0.1) == 10`
- **Double-only**: All computation done in `double`, causes issues with `float` inputs  
- **Default behavior**: Only uses relative comparison, so `Approx(0) == X` only works for `X == 0`

### Path Handling
❌ **Incorrect**:
```cpp
std::string path = TEST_DATA_DIR + "/model.obj";  // May have path separator issues
```

✅ **Correct**:
```cpp
std::string path = std::string(TEST_DATA_DIR) + "/model.obj";
// or use boost::filesystem for complex path operations
```

### Exception Testing
❌ **Incorrect**:
```cpp
bool threw_exception = false;
try {
    risky_function();
} catch (...) {
    threw_exception = true;
}
REQUIRE(threw_exception);
```

✅ **Correct**:
```cpp
REQUIRE_THROWS(risky_function());
// or for specific exceptions
REQUIRE_THROWS_AS(risky_function(), SpecificException);
```

### Thread Safety

⚠️ **CRITICAL**: Catch2 assertions are **NOT thread-safe** by default!

> **Note**: Catch2 v3.9.0+ has opt-in thread-safe assertions via `CATCH_CONFIG_EXPERIMENTAL_THREAD_SAFE_ASSERTIONS`. OrcaSlicer is on v3.11.0 but does not enable this flag, so assertions remain non-thread-safe by default.

❌ **Incorrect**: Will cause undefined behavior or crashes
```cpp
std::thread t([&]() {
    REQUIRE(threaded_operation() == expected);  // NOT THREAD-SAFE!
    CHECK(other_operation());                   // NOT THREAD-SAFE!
});
```

✅ **Correct**: Collect results, assert on main thread
```cpp
std::atomic<bool> success{false};
std::atomic<int> error_count{0};

std::thread t([&]() {
    // Do work in thread, collect results
    bool result1 = (threaded_operation() == expected);
    bool result2 = other_operation();
    
    if (result1 && result2) {
        success = true;
    } else {
        error_count++;
    }
});

t.join();

// Assert results on main thread
REQUIRE(success);
REQUIRE(error_count == 0);
```

#### Thread Safety Rules:
- **REQUIRE family**: Would terminate process in spawned threads (throws exception with no try-catch)
- **CHECK family**: Not thread-safe, can corrupt internal state
- **SKIP, FAIL, SUCCEED**: Not thread-safe even with v3 thread-safe assertions
- **Message macros**: INFO, CAPTURE, WARN - not thread-safe
- **STATIC_REQUIRE/CHECK**: Not thread-safe (relies on runtime registration)

I'm noting that upstream still has that one insertion point in push_notification_data, with in-place updates for certain kinds. Now I'm weighing a zero-footprint approach: keeping the existing fork lines as-is but generalizing the fork-owned function behind them so JusPrin can capture operation events without adding more upstream changes.

But the hook fires before the notification actually gets inserted, so a listener would need to defer reading the manager until after insertion via CallAfter, then diff the visited set against the prior one to detect new events. The tricky part is identity: using (type, text) as the diff key is fragile, since pushing the same type+text twice (like exporting to the same path again) would get merged or missed when the earlier notice closes and the new one looks identical — meaning the event could slip through undetected unless the hook itself tracks counts.

So I'm considering Option S1: modify the fork's own few lines so the hook call carries type and level directly instead of just text, which actually shrinks the footprint by one line and avoids adding a new call site. The concern now is keeping the fork header decoupled from NotificationManager.hpp — casting the enum to int to avoid a dependency, or forward-declaring the types instead.

But even with this change, the hook still misses several things: it won't catch actions/callbacks, progress updates and completion states for uploads/downloads that bypass the push path, close events, or in-place updates for the various bbl_show_* notifications beyond their initial push. I'm now wondering whether there's a better signal source than notifications for tracking upload progress specifically.

Checking how PrintHostJobQueue reports progress — it emits events that the PrintHostQueueDialog listens for, and the dialog's handlers then call into the notification manager setters. This means the fork could bind directly to those same queue dialog events instead of going through notifications, similar to how the monitor already binds Plater events elsewhere, requiring zero upstream changes. I need to verify these events are declared where I expect in the print host dialog header.

For Bambu's send flow, that uses its own dialog progress rather than the notification path. For downloads, there's a separate downloader event system handling web URL downloads from Printables or MakerWorld, which might matter later for JusPrin. For export completion, I need to trace through Plater's internals to find where that event actually originates.

I'm now thinking a two-tier proposal makes sense: Tier 1 covers events with rich data from real sources needing zero upstream changes (export finished, upload progress, slicing), while Tier 2 handles everything else pushed generically through the manager as type/level/text, surfaced as activity notices with a fork-owned classification table deciding whether to show, route to the print monitor, or drop each notification.

For hypertext-callback notices, I'm weighing whether to add an accessor like `activate_hypertext` or just hand the fork the data's hypertext string and callback directly, since those are accessible members within the manager's own function. The fork would then render the action label and invoke the callback, needing access to `m_evt_handler` as well to actually fire it.

But for subclass-specific actions like export's open-folder/eject, URL download, upload cancel, and sync conflict resolution, those buttons aren't captured in the generic callback at all -- so I need to figure out whether the fork can reimplement them using existing public APIs (removable drive manager's eject, printhost job queue's cancel) or whether the sync conflict callbacks are buried as constructor args to the subclass where they're not exposed.

Sync conflict is trickier since it ties to Orca Cloud preset sync, and whether that's even relevant to JusPrin is a product question for Kenneth, not an engineering one. My recommendation framing: decide which notification kinds actually matter first, then pick mechanism per kind -- a single upstream seam change to carry the kind/level/action through every push call, paired with a fork-owned classification table keyed on NotificationType, using an exhaustive switch with no default so the compiler warns via -Wswitch if upstream ever adds a new type.

That same classification table conveniently does double duty: it drives the surfacing/routing decision and also acts as the regression guard against unclassified enum values slipping through.

As for where things actually surface -- a transient toast near the canvas, the pill area, the header, or a chat system line -- that's a product/UI call I can't fully settle myself, but there's precedent: StatusRow already threads lines into the chat for filament-change events, so operation results like export completions could plausibly become durable chat system lines with inline actions, except the chat panel might be closed, which argues for also considering the pill area as a fallback. Export finished doesn't have its own dedicated event -- it fires the notification directly inside the completion handlers, so that push call is the capture point I need, using the export path and directory stored on the notification object itself.

I'm now hitting a wall passing the notification reference outward since PopNotification is a private nested class -- the fork can't name that type across the boundary. Rather than reconstructing the path from text parsing or app config lookups, the cleaner approach is to have the seam pass a generic callable wrapping the notification's on_text_click virtual, which for ExportFinishedNotification opens the containing folder -- letting the fork invoke the action without needing to know the concrete type.

But capturing a raw pointer to the notification is unsafe since it may be destroyed, so I'm thinking a safer upstream-neutral accessor would be a NotificationManager method that looks up a notification by type and invokes its action, closing it if needed. That gives the fork a type-based way to trigger the primary action for any notification kind, while the secondary "eject" action can just be handled directly via the removable drive manager's public API.

Weighing the combined minimal footprint for all three problems: the seam change nets zero lines, and I'd add a read-only visitor-style accessor that exposes type, level, and text for each active notification. This covers the "operation notices" case too, since many of those are lasting states in the manager that persist until explicitly closed or timed out — meaning polling the manager on a push signal could be sufficient instead of needing a full action-trigger API.

Given most notices have a defined lifetime (either a fixed duration or persistent), JusPrin could mirror the manager's live non-print notices into its own toast stack using the accessor plus a change signal from the existing push hook, paired with a lightweight timer to handle fade-outs while any mirrored notice is active. This way the fork doesn't own timing policy — it just reflects Orca's existing lifetime semantics — and notices stop being "unaskable" since they remain re-queryable from the manager for as long as they're alive.

In-place text updates are also visible by re-reading the text accessor, but progress percentages aren't, so those need tier-1 sources like upload progress instead. For actions like "activate," that's only relevant if JusPrin wants to trigger the native action itself — otherwise the main recommendation holds: mirror the manager via the same accessor, woken by the existing push hook, since that hook is fork-owned and can host a second listener without touching upstream code. Though I notice the hook's condition on non-empty text might exclude certain notices from being caught this way.

Actually, since every push already schedules an extra frame and the overlay renderer runs every frame, I don't even need a wake-up hook — the mirror can simply re-read the manager each time the overlay draws, piggybacking on Orca's existing frame scheduling with zero extra upstream lines beyond the accessor itself. I want to confirm this behavior holds at runtime.

P3(b)'s classification test over the enum means unclassified kinds still surface by default — warning/error show as plate-wide raw-text issues, lower levels as generic toasts — so new upstream kinds stay visible rather than silent. But I need to worry about shared kinds like SlicingError, which spans both slice failures and canvas errors; since specific readers already claim that kind, the catch-all must skip it to avoid double-reporting, raising the question of how to handle a kind split between claimed and unclaimed producers.

PlaterError illustrates this: it covers both the "object over edge" case (claimed) and unrelated mesh-boolean export failures (unclaimed), yet Orca's notification system only allows one PlaterError notice to exist at a time, so these texts clobber each other natively. That means for shared single-instance kinds, the catch-all could work by comparing the notice's current displayed text against the text the specific reader would have produced, since both come from the same Orca string source.

That's dedupe-by-text rather than identity-by-id, which conflicts with the rule that identity must never be derived from message text — so I'd flag it as a judgment call rather than a clean answer. The alternative is to just treat shared kinds as always-claimed and skip the catch-all for them entirely, accepting that unclaimed producers sharing that kind slip through uncaught.

Similarly for SlicingError, which also isn't a multi-instance type: readers mapping to slice failure, toolpath or height out-of-bounds, TPU error, or non-printable filament would explain it, otherwise catch-all shows it. I should verify the "single instance" assumption against the actual activate_existing logic, confirming it rotates and updates when type matches and isn't in the multiple-types set, and I could cheaply test this in the harness too — but I'm running low on context to keep digging further.

Given limited context budget left, I should stop reading large files and focus on running experiments and writing up results. content.thinking:
The git cat-file blob command failed with a "bad file" error, so the subsequent file/python commands never ran — meaning the stale GLCanvas3D_pub.hpp file got used instead, even though the stat output showed thousands of insertions and deletions.

Then it hits me: `$C1:src` is getting mangled by zsh's colon-path history modifier trap, where `$VAR:path` triggers substitution modifiers like `:s`. That explains why the earlier `git show $C1:src/...` also broke, while `$U:$f` worked fine since `:$` isn't a recognized modifier. The fix is to wrap the variable in braces as `${C1}` to avoid the colon trap entirely.

content.thinking:
Both simulations check out cleanly: the accessor commit adds 9 lines across 2 files with an identical conflict list and correct merge, and the flushpublic commit adds 2 lines in 1 file with the same clean result. Now I'm double-checking whether my earlier accessor simulation might have been thrown off by a colon-handling quirk in how I referenced the commit when building the tree and hashing the file.

Looking at the diff stat confirms the 7+2=9 insertion count is correct. There's a semantic benefit to calling upstream's function rather than copying it: when upstream later improves the flushing-error check logic, a caller automatically inherits that improvement, whereas a copy would not.

Now I'm working through the seam generalisation question for push_notification_data -- specifically whether the text1 check inside the notification guard needs to change. I conclude the mirror-via-accessor approach requires no change to this seam, so I'm reasoning through how to phrase that evaluation given the task explicitly asks whether the seam can be generalised with minimal upstream footprint.

I'm noting the seam could pass kind and level info with zero net new lines since it reuses the fork's existing site, which has had minimal upstream churn since the fork base. But the seam only fires on first notification push, missing in-place updates, progress, and close events, and it runs before insertion -- so it's insufficient on its own for tracking ongoing state. My recommendation leans toward leaving the seam unchanged, relying on the accessor for current state and Orca's frame scheduling for wake-ups, treating the seam at most as an optional trigger. I'm still planning to simulate a two-line variant of the check anyway just to get a concrete conflict count for comparison.

Build progress is slow, only 17 steps in those four minutes, so at this rate the remaining steps could take around 80 minutes. Rather than waiting idle, I'll use the time to write the report, build out the inventory, and start prototyping the P3 guard-test that checks classification coverage against the enums.

For the test design, I'm considering a fork-owned mapping table that classifies each NotificationType and GLCanvas3D::EWarning value into categories. The strongest approach is using a switch statement without a default case combined with -Werror=switch, so the build itself fails when a new enumerator appears unhandled; for NotificationType there's a count sentinel I could pair with a static_assert to force a compile failure on upstream changes, though EWarning lacks an equivalent sentinel and I need to check its visibility inside GLCanvas3D first.

I plan to compile a classifier into fork code using an exhaustive switch with diagnostics escalated to errors for both GCC/clang and MSVC, so that when upstream adds a new notification kind, the fork build breaks immediately at that file—exactly the "stop on conflict" behavior fork stewardship wants. To prove this fails first, I want to simulate it by copying upstream's current enum into a scratch file with the classifier and confirming it doesn't compile cleanly until the new case is handled.

But compile-time safety only catches enum changes, not new callers reusing existing kinds with different content (like a new push_plater_warning call with new text but an unchanged enum value). For that gap I need a runtime catch-all to handle unknown producers gracefully, since the build break alone won't catch content-level additions that don't touch the enum itself.

I'm also considering a third safeguard: a post-rebase check that greps and counts push-notification call sites against a checked-in baseline number, so if someone adds a new caller the count mismatch flags it for review -- similar to how source-scanning guard tests exist for things like brand tokens. I want to prototype the compile-time enum check standalone first since it's the cheapest to verify.

Now I'm checking whether `enum class EWarning` in GLCanvas3D is actually accessible outside that class, since the switch-based safeguard depends on being able to reference it.

entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

# Inventory of OrcaSlicer notice kinds

Appendix to `investigation-print-issues-four-gaps.md`. Untracked on purpose.

Source: the `NotificationType` enum in `src/slic3r/GUI/NotificationManager.hpp` at `jusprin-newui` commit `570e3fb1c7` (62 kinds plus the count sentinel), and a search of every caller of the notification manager's `push_*` and `bbl_show_*` functions in `src/slic3r` (102 call sites outside the manager itself). "Lasting" means OrcaSlicer keeps the notice until it closes it itself; a number is the seconds before it fades. "JusPrin today" was checked by searching the fork's own code for any use of the notification manager: there is none except the file-load hook, so anything not listed as shown is shown nowhere while the shell is installed.

Route is my proposed classification:

- **Issue**: a print problem; belongs in the print-issue list.
- **Toast**: the result of something the person just did; a short-lived JusPrin confirmation.
- **Progress**: long-running work with a cancel; belongs with slicing progress in the header.
- **App**: application or account state; belongs on Home or in Preferences, not in a project.
- **None**: not shown.

## Print problems (states that can be asked again)

| Kind | Pushed by | Lasting? | Action on the notice | JusPrin today | Route |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `ValidateError` | `Plater` after `Print::validate` (2 sites) | Lasting | "Jump to [object] (setting)" | Issue list | Issue (covered) |
| `ValidateWarning` | `Plater` (1 site) | Lasting | Same | Issue list | Issue (covered) |
| `SlicingError` | `Plater` when a slice fails; `GLCanvas3D` for path outside the plate, path above the height, and its generic errors | Lasting | "Jump to [object]" | Issue list | Issue (covered). Shared between producers |
| `SlicingSeriousWarning` | `GLCanvas3D`, G-code path conflict | Lasting | "Jump to [object]" | Issue list | Issue (covered) |
| `SlicingWarning` | `Plater`, slicing step warnings | Lasting | "Jump to [object]" | Issue list | Issue (covered) |
| `PlaterError` | `GLCanvas3D` (copy over the edge, SLA supports outside); `Plater::validate_current_plate`; `Plater.cpp` near line 15446 (mesh boolean failed during export); `GUI_ObjectList.cpp` 3292 (mesh combine failed) | Lasting | None | Edge case only | Issue for the edge; the two mesh failures are operation errors with no surface. Shared between producers |
| `LeftExtruderUnprintableError`, `RightExtruderUnprintableError` | `GLCanvas3D` and `Plater::validate_current_plate` | Lasting | "Click here to regroup" (opens the nozzle mapping dialog) | Issue list (words only) | Issue (covered; the action is lost) |
| `PlaterWarning` | `GLCanvas3D` (prime tower outside, filament mixture, "Only the object being edited is visible", object limited); `Plater.cpp` 17964; `GLGizmoMeshBoolean.cpp` (3 warnings from the boolean tool) | Lasting. Several at once, told apart by text | None | Prime tower and mixture only | Issue for those two; the rest have no surface. Shared between producers |
| `BBLFlushingVolumeZero` | `GLCanvas3D` | Lasting | "Flushing Volume" (opens the dialog) | **Nowhere** (problem 2) | Issue |
| `BBLFilamentPrintableError` | `GLCanvas3D` | Lasting | "Click here to regroup" | Issue list | Issue (covered) |
| `BBLSliceLimitError` | `GLCanvas3D`, after slicing | Lasting | "Click here to regroup" | Issue list | Issue (covered) |
| `BBLSliceMultiExtruderHeightOutside` | `GLCanvas3D`, after slicing | Lasting | None | Issue list | Issue (covered) |
| `BBLBedFilamentIncompatible` | `GLCanvas3D`, after slicing | Lasting | "Click for more." (wiki) | Issue list | Issue (covered) |
| `BBLMixUsePLAAndPETG` | `GLCanvas3D` | Lasting | "Click Wiki for help." | Issue list | Issue (covered) |
| `BBLNozzleFilamentIncompatible` | `GLCanvas3D` | Lasting | None | Issue list | Issue (covered) |
| `BBLSeqPrintInfo` | `Plater::config_change_notification` ("Print By Object: suggest auto-arrange") | 10 days | None | Nowhere | Toast, or drop: it is advice |
| `BBLSliceEmptyLayer`, `BBLNeedSupportON`, `BBLGcodeOverlap` | No caller in this version; the functions exist | n/a | None | n/a | Issue if upstream starts calling them |

## Results of something the person just did (events)

| Kind | Pushed by | Lasting? | Action | JusPrin today | Route |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `ExportFinished` | `Plater` export paths (4 sites, including "sent to the printer's storage") and `push_import_finished_notification` ("Model file downloaded.") | 20 s; lasting when written to a removable drive | Open containing folder; Eject | Nowhere. The header's "Export sliced file…" ends with no confirmation | Toast with Open folder and Eject |
| `ExportOngoing` | `Plater`, 1 s after an export starts | Until the export ends | None | Nowhere | Progress |
| `CustomNotification` | 16 sites: drive ejected or eject failed (`Plater`), calibration INFO lines (`Plater`), bundle updated, downloaded, removed, no longer available, unauthorized (`GUI_App`, 9 sites), "Syncing presets from cloud…" (`MainFrame`), malformed download URL (`Downloader`), SLA archive without presets (`SLAImportJob`), objects that did not fit an arrange (`ArrangeJob`) | 10 s; errors lasting | None | Only those raised during a file load, which the file-load hook sends to the chat | Toast. One kind for unrelated facts, so it cannot be routed more finely |
| `BBLPlateInfo` | `ArrangeJob`, `OrientJob`: "This plate is locked", "No arrangeable objects are selected", "Object has zero size" | 10 days | None | Nowhere. An arrange that is refused looks like nothing happened | Toast |
| `ArrangeOngoing` | `ArrangeJob` | Until the job ends | None | Nowhere | Progress |
| `BBLGeneralError` | `Plater.cpp` 15476 and 15543, mesh combine failures | Lasting | None | Nowhere | Toast (error) |
| `CgalFinished` | `GUI_ObjectList`, repair finished | 5 s | None | Nowhere, unless the agent's repair tool reports it | Toast |
| `CustomSupportsAndSeamRemovedAfterRepair` | `Plater` (paint removed before repair); `GLGizmosManager` reuses it for "Error: Please close all toolbar menus first" | 10 s | None | Nowhere | Toast |
| `UpdatedItemsInfo` | `GUI_ObjectList`, cut connectors | 10 s | None | Nowhere | Toast |
| `EmptyColorChangeCode` | The layer slider in Check print | 10 s | None | Nowhere | Toast |
| `MmSegmentationExceededExtrudersLimit` | The colour painting tool | 10 s | None | Nowhere | Toast |
| `UnknownFont` | The text tool | Varies | None | Nowhere | Toast |
| `BBL3MFInfo` | `Plater` while loading a 3MF | 10 days | None | Chat, through the file-load hook | Covered |
| `BBLPreviewOnlyMode` | `Plater`, a G-code-only file was loaded | Lasting | None | Nowhere | Toast or a header state |

## Long-running work

| Kind | Pushed by | Lasting? | Action | JusPrin today | Route |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `SlicingProgress` | `Plater` | While slicing | Cancel; export link when done | Header | Covered |
| `ProgressIndicator` | The `Plater`'s job worker (arrange, orient, repair and the other background jobs) | While a job runs | Cancel | Nowhere: job progress and its Cancel are invisible | Progress |
| `PrintHostUpload` | `PrintHostDialogs.cpp`, one per upload to a network printer | Until done; errors stay | Cancel; error state | Nowhere | Progress. Better read from the upload queue's own public events (`EVT_PRINTHOST_PROGRESS`, `_ERROR`, `_CANCEL`) than from the notice |
| `URLDownload` | `Downloader` | Until done | Pause, cancel, open | Nowhere | Progress. `Downloader`'s public events carry the same facts |

## Application and account state

| Kind | Pushed by | Lasting? | Action | JusPrin today | Route |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `NewAppAvailable` | Call commented out in `GUI_App`; one wrapper with no caller | 20 s | Download page | n/a | None |
| `PresetUpdateAvailable` | `PresetUpdater` | 10 days | "Detail." | Nowhere | App |
| `PresetUpdateFinished` | `PresetUpdater` | 20 s | None | Nowhere | App |
| `BBLPluginUpdateAvailable` | `PresetUpdater` (2 sites) | 10 days | "Details" | Nowhere | App |
| `BBLPrinterConfigUpdateAvailable` | `PresetUpdater` | 10 days | "Details" | Nowhere | App |
| `BBLPluginInstallHint` | `Plater`, network plug-in not detected | Lasting | "Click here to install it." | The printer setup chat explains the missing plug-in when asked | App |
| `BBLUserPresetExceedLimit` | `GUI_App` | 10 days | "Wiki Guide" | Nowhere | App |
| `OrcaSharedProfilesAvailable` | `Plater` | Lasting | Browse; don't show again | Nowhere | App, or None |
| `OrcaSyncConflict` | `GUI_App`, preset sync conflict | Lasting | Two buttons: pull, or force push (delete in one case) | Nowhere. The conflict cannot be resolved while the shell is installed | App. The two actions live in a notice subclass, not in the generic link |
| `DidYouKnowHint` | `GUI_App` at start when hints are on | 300 s | Next and previous tip | Nowhere | None (decision) |
| `Mouse3dDisconnected` | `Mouse3DController` | 10 s | None | Nowhere | Toast or None |
| `DesktopIntegrationSuccess`, `UndoDesktopIntegrationSuccess` | The Linux desktop integration dialog | 10 s | None | Nowhere | None |
| `BBLObjectInfo` | `Plater` (2 sites): the object size card; with "(Repair)" when the mesh has open edges | 10 days | "(Repair)" | Nowhere | Decision: the open-edges case is a defective-geometry fact |
| `SimplifySuggestion` | The simplify tool, for very large meshes | 10 s | "Simplify model" | Nowhere | Toast or None |

## Declared but never pushed in this version

`NewAlphaAvailable`, `NewBetaAvailable`, `ProgressBar`, `EmptyAutoColorChange`, `SignDetected` (closed in one place, pushed nowhere), `QuitSLAManualMode` (referenced by the SLA tool only), `DesktopIntegrationFail`, `UndoDesktopIntegrationFail`, `OrcaCloudAPIError`.

## What upstream has added since the fork base

Fork base `3ffb9585d2` (2026-06-18), upstream `b3490a1cdc` (2026-10-09):

- 6 new kinds: `BBLSingleExtruderMixedFilamentRisk` and `BBLMixedFilamentBroken` (print problems), and four plug-in errors (`OrcaCloudPluginMissingError`, `OrcaLocalPluginMissingError`, `OrcaPluginInactiveError`, `OrcaPluginCapabilityUnavailableError`).
- 1 new canvas warning: `GLCanvas3D::EWarning::SingleExtruderMixedFilament`.
- Call sites that push a notice: 102 at the fork base, 125 upstream now. 19 of the 23 new ones are plain `push_notification(...)` calls, which add no enum value.
- The two enums were each touched by 15 upstream commits in the last two years.
